title: He Xiaopeng: Large Models Are Bad for Small Companies — Stronger Means More Data, More Data Means More Cost
dek: The network effect of big AI is: stronger means more data, more data means more cost, more cost means you have to sell more cars to support the system.
why: He Xiaopeng rarely lays out the engineering details of putting autonomous-driving large models into production, the scale of training costs, and why he thinks large models are bad for small car companies.
who: Founders, investors and automaker practitioners focused on autonomous driving and large-model deployment, especially those who want the engineering details and the cost threshold.
skip: The opening discussion of seating and colors at the Xiaomi SU7 launch can be fast-forwarded.

points.h: The dimension where large models can actually make money is autonomous driving
points.body: He Xiaopeng judges that language large models have basically not made money — apart from NVIDIA or something like Microsoft, OpenAI raised money rather than earned it. He believes the other dimension where large models can genuinely make money is AD, autonomous driving: raise autonomous-driving capability 50x to 100x, turn assisted driving into fully autonomous driving or near driverless, and users will be willing to pay. His reasoning: users won't buy a piece of software or a service for tens of thousands of yuan on its own, but spending 100,000-plus, 200,000-plus or 300,000-plus yuan on a car they like that includes this capability is a very high possibility.

points.h: Autonomous-driving large models need brakes and a goalkeeper
points.body: He Xiaopeng distinguishes two directions for large models: language large models don't pursue reliability or robustness — if they get it wrong, no way, don't care; autonomous driving is different, if it gets it wrong you have to preserve safety, so you need a controller, you need brakes. He explains that XPeng could adopt the new-generation technology relatively quickly because its previous-generation autonomous-driving capability was strong enough that you could take the previous generation, tweak it, and turn it into a controller; with a controller and safety brakes, the new generation reaches greater strength on certain capabilities, and the weak spots are repaired and compensated for with the controller and brakes.

points.h: Putting large models in cars means rewriting the data-flow logic
points.body: He Xiaopeng says deployment is not releasing some model; it is the team reading the papers, understanding the architecture, then rewriting the data-flow logic according to the logic of large models, adding data collection, doing pre-training, training out an engine, and then testing in a simulation environment. At the very beginning the simulation results were extremely poor — what they wrote was completely unusable — and the most important thing was that the data volume was not large: traditional programming assumes 100 million scenarios for a right turn, and you can at least cover 1 million to 10 million of them, but a large model cannot cover the first 1 million scenarios, and for a long time it is still 0. The core is data volume and enormous training; he reveals that training costs in the second half of this year are over 100 million US dollars.

points.h: The network effect of big AI is bad for small companies
points.body: He Xiaopeng says intelligence will form a very technical network effect: in big AI, the stronger you are, the more data you have; the more data you have, the more cost you have; the more cost you have, the more cars you have to sell to support the system. When a supply chain sells you something, it's a piece of software I made and I sell to you, but it doesn't require continuous training — otherwise that cost is a joke. But many future collaborations around large models must last a length of time, and be very large. So in a certain sense large models are unfavorable to small companies, because their time cost, business logic, R&D barriers and training costs are all thresholds. He mentions XPeng's 3.5 billion yuan a year of AI investment, which most companies cannot do.

points.h: Replicating FSD takes tens of billions and only a 5% chance of success
points.body: Asked how much money, how much time and which foundational elements are needed to replicate Tesla's end-to-end FSD, He Xiaopeng says tens of billions. First you need a very large amount of money, then you need super-strong people — it is absolutely not something an ordinary programmer can do with algorithms; you need many cars running on the roads, you need the entire execution capability to turn, and the time to turn is also very long, and the probability is also very low. He draws an analogy to the probability of startup success: if you invest tens of billions, several years and a thousand people, and the probability of success is only 5%, will you invest — that is one of the thresholds. Putting in money only means it is possible to succeed, it does not mean it can succeed.

points.h: The US-China AI gap is widening, and acceleration is the key
points.body: On this trip He Xiaopeng spent two weeks in the US across nine cities, and judges that the US-China gap in AI is widening. On last year's trip he saw many people in Silicon Valley pivoting to AI, but had not yet seen AI's changes; across three trips spanning more than a year, the changes are bigger than imagined. This time he looked at both Tesla and Waymo: Waymo has not yet pivoted to large models and still uses its original algorithm system; previously using Waymo felt far ahead of Tesla, but this time it is obvious that acceleration is the most important point. He says people use a traditional linear speed, using past experience in their heads, to look at the speed of technological development, but in large-model-oriented AI, the speed of technological change is starting to accelerate.

points.h: Large models have not lowered the barriers to autonomous driving
points.body: Someone asked whether large models have lowered the barriers to autonomous driving, and whether it is just a matter of piling up chips; He Xiaopeng disagrees. He gives the layers: below compute is something called BOM; above compute there is the model, or OS; above OS is data; above data there is globalization and globalized policy; above that is experience. He says no one can just take an ordinary large model and run autonomous driving with it, because all models today, frankly, look at things from a non-real-time, low-reliability angle, but autonomous driving is different — it needs millisecond level, at least hundred-millisecond or even ten-millisecond level. Data is also very hard; every OEM's master's-level work starts over, and how do you satisfy the global scope and policies and regulations.

points.h: The chance of FSD doing Robot Taxi within a year is zero
points.body: Asked about the logic that once FSD's Robot Taxi lands, a Tesla at 30,000 US dollars taking 20 orders a day pays for itself in 75 days, He Xiaopeng says this logic holds in the long run but not in the next few years, because there will be all kinds of additional problems. He completely does not believe FSD will be able to do anything on Robot Taxi within the next year; it might be implemented in a local scenario, but the larger-scale, better-executed version everyone imagines — he thinks the probability is zero. He cites his own experience this time riding Waymo and taking over twice — actually it was not him taking over, it was the cloud taking over twice; you need a cloud-based management system, and different countries and different regions are completely different.

quotes.text: Today, for autonomous driving, if you invest tens of billions, several years and a thousand people, and the probability of success is only 5%, will you invest — that is one of the thresholds. So putting in money only means it is possible to succeed, it does not mean it can succeed.

People use a traditional linear speed, using past experience in their heads, interesting or unintentional, to look at the speed of technological development, but today in large-model-oriented AI, I think the speed of technological change is starting to accelerate.
